title: Full Spec MCP: Hidden Capabilities of the MCP spec — Harald Kirschner, Microsoft/VSCode

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is MCP protocol design, tool calling, sampling, elicitations, and integrating external systems through the full spec. MCP is a developer-facing protocol for building AI integrations used by software builders in tools like VS Code. The talk covers building MCP servers (development) and deploying them in production clients like VS Code (deployment). The talk assumes familiarity with MCP primitives and function calling, targeting developers building MCP implementations. A conference presentation from the AI Engineer channel demonstrating MCP spec capabilities with live demos. summary: Harald Kirschner from Microsoft/VSCode presents on the hidden capabilities of the MCP specification, emphasizing that the ecosystem is still in its earliest stages—the MCP steering committee met in person for the first time just 10 days prior. A key problem is the 'MCP is just another API wrapper' syndrome: developers focus exclusively on tools because they yield immediate success, creating a reinforcing loop. Technical barriers include missing support in clients, SDKs, and documentation. VS Code's upcoming v1.10 release (in insiders) achieves full spec support, having started with tools two months ago and progressively added discovery and roots. Tools map to function calling but suffer from quality problems identified in LangChain research: too many tools, too many tool domains, and excessive repetition all confuse AI. VS Code addresses this with per-chat tool selection, tool mentioning, and upcoming user-defined tool sets. Dynamic tool discovery allows servers to provide context-appropriate tools on the fly, demonstrated with a MUD dungeon crawler. Resources provide a semantic layer for returning file references rather than giant payloads, enabling context-aware customization like detecting Python environments and frameworks. Sampling allows servers to request LLM completions from the client (wired to GPT-4.1), enabling progressive enhancements. Developer experience improvements include a dev mode with debugger attachment for Python and Node. Spec evolution highlights include updated auth spec, streamable HTTP (lacking server implementations), and a community registry effort on GitHub. Kirschner introduces elicitations—an upcoming spec feature allowing tools to reach back to the user for direct input when more information is needed, adding statefulness to tools. He closes with a strong call to action: build action-oriented, context-aware, semantic-aware servers using the full spec; read open RFCs like namespaces and search; file issues to influence client and SDK roadmaps; and advocate for full-spec adoption including sampling. The ecosystem is fast-moving and interoperability gaps will close as more users showcase stateful servers and provide feedback.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction to MCP and its Current State
sections.summary: MCP ecosystem is very early; steering committee first met in person 10 days ago at MCP Dev Summit. Full spec has roots, sampling, prompts, tools, and resources for rich interactions, but there's a gap in implementation.

sections.title: The 'MCP is just another API wrapper' Syndrome
sections.summary: Developers focus on tools for immediate success, creating a reinforcing loop. Technical barriers include missing support in clients, SDKs, and documentation. Most adoption goes to tools.

sections.title: VS Code's Full Spec Support
sections.summary: VS Code launched MCP support 2 months ago with tools, then added discovery and roots. v1.10 (in insiders) achieves full spec support.

sections.title: Challenges with Tools and Solutions
sections.summary: Tool quality problems from too many tools, domains, and repetition per LangChain research. Solutions include per-chat tool selection, tool mentioning, user-defined tool sets, and dynamic tool discovery demonstrated with a MUD dungeon crawler game.

sections.title: Resources and Their Importance
sections.summary: Resources provide semantic layer for file references, Python environment detection, package/library detection for framework customization, and CI/CD pipeline context without repeatedly asking users.

sections.title: Sampling
sections.summary: Server requests LLM completions from client; permission dialogue appears; wired to GPT-4.1 by default; enables summarization, website-to-markdown, agentic server tools as progressive enhancements.

sections.title: Developer Experience Improvements
sections.summary: VS Code dev mode with console logging and debugger attachment with breakpoints for Python and Node, addressing the challenge of debugging servers owned by client/host processes.

sections.title: Staying Updated with the Spec
sections.summary: Updated auth spec for enterprise-grade authorization; streamable HTTP available for two VS Code versions but lacking server implementations; SSE still possible with HTTP.

sections.title: Key Upcoming Features and Community Efforts
sections.summary: Community registry for server discovery is underway on GitHub at model context protocol registry. Elicitations—an upcoming spec draft feature—will allow tools to reach back to users for direct input when more information is needed, adding statefulness to tools. Steering committee and community working groups are collaboratively evolving the ecosystem.

sections.title: Call to Action
sections.summary: Progressive enhancement in MCP is possible now with full-spec clients available. Build action-oriented, context-aware, semantic-aware servers. Contribute by reading open RFCs (namespaces, search), following issues in SDKs, and filing feedback—VS Code reads all MCP issues and uses them to drive its roadmap. Advocate for full-spec adoption including sampling. VS Code team members Tyler and Rob available at Microsoft booth.

limitations: Missing support in clients, SDKs, documentation creates technical barriers to full spec adoption
Most implementations focus only on tools because resources and prompts can achieve similar flows
Sampling lacks structured formatting improvements—no implementations existed before VS Code insiders
Streamable HTTP lacks server implementations despite client support
Server discovery remains an unsolved pain point requiring community registry effort
Debugging MCP servers is difficult because servers are owned by client/host processes, not run manually
Interoperability gap exists between spec potential and client/server implementations
Elicitations not yet available—coming in next spec draft
